title: California Low Cost Auto Insurance Program: Who Qualifies, What the 10/20/3 Policy Covers, and How to Apply
description: California's Low Cost Auto program gives income-eligible drivers legal liability coverage. Eligibility, the 10/20/3 limits, gaps to know and how to apply.
author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: The California Low Cost Auto Insurance Program (CLCA) is a real state program, created under Insurance Code section 11629.7 and administered by the California Automobile Assigned Risk Plan.
Eligibility: household income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, a vehicle worth $25,000 or less, age 16 or older, a valid California license and a good driving record.
CLCA policies carry 10/20/3 liability, below the regular 30/60/15 minimum, but they are legal evidence of financial responsibility for enrolled drivers.
CLCA covers injuries and damage you cause to others, not your own car.
Apply at mylowcostauto.com, by phone at 1-866-602-8861, or through a certified agent.

faqs.question: Who qualifies for low cost auto insurance in California?
faqs.answer: Drivers 16 or older with a valid California license, household income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, a vehicle worth $25,000 or less, and a good driving record.

faqs.question: Is California low cost auto insurance legal coverage?
faqs.answer: Yes. Although its 10/20/3 limits are below the standard 30/60/15, it is valid evidence of financial responsibility for enrolled drivers.

faqs.question: Does CLCA cover damage to my own car?
faqs.answer: No. The base policy is liability only. Physical damage coverage is a separate decision; see [comprehensive vs collision](/compare/comprehensive-vs-collision).

faqs.question: How do I apply for the California Low Cost Auto program?
faqs.answer: Visit mylowcostauto.com, call 1-866-602-8861, or find a certified agent. You will need proof of income, your license and vehicle details.

content.text: California's minimum liability rose to 30/60/15 in 2025, and for many lower-income drivers the price of staying legal rose with it. The state's answer is a genuine program, not an ad: the California Low Cost Auto Insurance Program. Unlike the 'program' marketing Florida drivers run into (see [Florida compliant drivers program](/learn/florida-compliant-drivers-program)), this one is written into state law. It is part of the compliance picture laid out in our [state auto insurance compliance guide](/learn/state-auto-insurance-compliance-guide).

rows: At or below 250% of the federal poverty level
Valid California driver's license (drivers with less than 3 years' experience became eligible in 2015)
Must meet the program's good driver definition

content.text: The base policy is liability only: $10,000 for injury or death to one person, $20,000 per accident, and $3,000 for property damage. Those limits are lower than the regular 30/60/15 minimum, but for enrolled drivers they count as valid evidence of financial responsibility, which is what police and the DMV check (see [California evidence of liability insurance](/learn/california-evidence-of-liability-insurance)). Additional coverage is available for an extra charge.

content.title: Legal, but Thin
content.text: $3,000 in property damage won't cover most bumper-and-headlight repairs on a newer car, and nothing in the base policy pays for your own vehicle. CLCA keeps you legal and avoids registration suspension; it does not make a crash affordable. Read [what happens if you crash without insurance](/qa/what-happens-if-you-crash-without-insurance) to see how excess judgments are collected.

items: Check eligibility and get a quote at mylowcostauto.com or by calling 1-866-602-8861.
Gather proof of household income (such as tax returns or benefit letters), your license and vehicle details.
Complete the application online or with a certified CLCA agent near you.
Once the policy is issued, keep the ID card on paper or your phone; it is your proof at traffic stops.

content.text: Why Staying Insured Matters More Than the Price

Driving uninsured in California can mean a ticket of a few hundred dollars after penalty assessments (see [what happens if you can't show proof of insurance in California](/qa/california-no-proof-of-insurance-ticket)). After an accident, it can mean a license suspension of up to four years, with an SR-22 filing to get it back, as explained in [do you have to report an accident to the California DMV](/qa/california-sr1-accident-report). A CLCA policy costs far less than either outcome.
